{{nihongo|'''Inamura Shrine'''|稲村神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Hitachi Province]].

=== Enshrined deities ===
The shrine enshrines the following 12 deities:
* {{ill|Nigihayahi|Q10949054|qid=Q10949054|lt=Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto}} – ancestor of the {{ill|Mononobe clan|Q1755836|qid=Q1755836}}.
* 11 deities of the {{ill|Kamiyonanayo|es|Kamiyonanayo|fr|Kamiyonanayo|hy|Կամիյոնանայո|it|Kamiyonanayo|ja|神世七代|ko|가미노요나나오|mni|ꯀꯃꯤꯌꯣꯅꯅꯌꯣ|pl|Kamiyonanayo|ru|Камиёнанаё|vi|Kamiyo-nanayo|zh|神世七代|qid=Q3275893}}

=== History ===
=== Foundation ===
[[File:Bontenyama-kofun zenkei.JPG|thumb|220px|right|{{center|{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Bontenyama Kofun}}}}{{small|According to one tradition, the tomb of Funase no Sukune, the first {{ill|Kuji Kokuzō|Q11369664|qid=Q11369664}}.}}]]
It is widely believed that the area where Inamura Shrine stands was the stronghold of the {{ill|Kuji Kokuzō|Q11369664|qid=Q11369664}} before the {{ill|Ritsuryō|Q742460|qid=Q742460}}. According to the “{{ill|Kokuzo Hongi|ja|国造本紀|qid=Q133833194}}” section of the {{ill|Kujiki|Q2716751|qid=Q2716751}}<ref group="original">Sendai Kuji Hongi, “Kokuzō Hongi,” entry on Kuji no Kuni no Miyatsuko.</ref>, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Seimu|ar|الإمبراطور سيمو|arz|الامبراطور سيمو|azb|سیمو (ایمپیراتور)|ca|Seimu|cs|Seimu|de|Seimu|es|Seimu Tennō|fa|امپراتور سیمو|fi|Seimu|fr|Seimu|hr|Seimu|hu|Szeimu japán császár|id|Kaisar Seimu|it|Seimu|ja|成務天皇|ka|სეიმუ|ko|세이무 천황|nl|Seimu|pl|Seimu|pt|Seimu|ru|Император Сэйму|sh|Car Seimu|simple|Emperor Seimu|sl|Cesar Sejmu|sv|Seimu|th|จักรพรรดิเซมุ|tl|Emperador Seimu|tr|Seimu (imparator)|uk|Імператор Сейму|uz|Imperator Seimu|vi|Thiên hoàng Seimu|yo|Emperor Seimu|zh|成務天皇|zh_min_nan|Seimu Thian-hông|zh_yue|成務天皇|qid=Q316672}}, Funase no Sukune, a third-generation descendant of Ikashikoo no Mikoto (a distant ancestor of the {{ill|Mononobe clan|Q1755836|qid=Q1755836|lt=Mononobe no Muraji}}), was appointed as the first Kuji no Kuni no Miyatsuko. Shrine tradition holds that at the time of this appointment, Funase no Sukune enshrined his ancestral deity {{ill|Nigihayahi|Q10949054|qid=Q10949054|lt=Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto}}. Because a “heavenly deity” or seven sacred mirrors were enshrined, the shrine came to be called “Seven-Generation Tenjin” {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Another tradition says that when {{ill|Yamato Takeru|Q461258|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto}} campaigned eastward, he enshrined the spirits of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Seven Generations of the Heavenly Deities}} at this site {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

To the southwest of Inamura Shrine lies the {{ill|Bontenyama-kofungun|ja|梵天山古墳群|qid=Q17220423}}. Its main tumulus, Bontenyama Kofun, is the second largest in Ibaraki Prefecture, and there is a tradition identifying it as the tomb of Funase no Sukune<ref>“Bontenyama Kofun Cluster,” Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei 8: Place Names of Ibaraki Prefecture, Heibonsha, 1982.</ref>.

=== Overview ===
In the {{ill|Rikkokushi|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168|lt=official histories}}, an entry states that in the second year of {{ill|Kashō|Q1373157|qid=Q1373157}} ({{ill|849|Q23902|qid=Q23902}})<ref group="original" name="Kashō 2"/> “Inamura no Kami” was placed under official offerings as a government shrine and displayed miraculous powers in times of flood and drought {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Later, in the second year of {{ill|Gangyō|Q747451|qid=Q747451}} ({{ill|878|Q23910|qid=Q23910}})<ref group="original" name="Gangyō 2"/>, its {{ill|Shinkai (divine rank)|Q11591025|qid=Q11591025}} was raised to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, and in the first year of {{ill|Ninna|Q1346317|qid=Q1346317}} ({{ill|885|Q24894|qid=Q24894}})<ref group="original" name="Ninna 1"/> it was further promoted to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ar|إنجيشيكي (كتاب ياباني)|de|Engishiki|es|Engishiki|fr|Engishiki|he|אנגישיקי|id|Engishiki|it|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|ko|엔기시키|min|Engishiki|mr|इंगिशिकी|nl|Engishiki|pt|Engishiki|ru|Энгисики|simple|Engishiki|tr|Engishiki|uk|Енґісікі|zh|延喜式|qid=Q1342448}} {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=register of shrines}} compiled in the fifth year of {{ill|Enchō|Q1327274|qid=Q1327274}} ({{ill|927|Q30470|qid=Q30470}}), it is listed as “Inamura Shrine” in {{ill|Kuji District, Ibaraki|ceb|Kuji-gun|es|Distrito de Kuji (Ibaraki)|fr|District de Kuji|id|Distrik Kuji, Ibaraki|it|Distretto di Kuji|ja|久慈郡|ko|구지군|pl|Powiat Kuji|th|อำเภอคูจิ|uk|Повіт Кудзі|vi|Kuji, Ibaraki|zh|久慈郡|qid=Q1075212}}, {{ill|Hitachi Province|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353}}, and ranked as a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}. However, there are other {{ill|Shikinai Ronsha|Q135022904|qid=Q135022904}} for this “Inamura no Kami”<ref group="note">These include {{ill|Chikata Shrine (Kanda)|Q54153265|qid=Q54153265}} in Daigo Town, Kuji District, Ibaraki Prefecture, and {{ill|Isobe inamura Shrine|Q65681696|qid=Q65681696}} in Sakuragawa City, Ibaraki Prefecture. The former is thought to be located in Mutsu Province, and the latter, while in Hitachi Province, is not in Kuji District.</ref>.

According to the *Newly Compiled Gazetteer of Hitachi Province*, when {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|Q1194944|qid=Q1194944}} passed through Tenjinbayashi Village in the fourth year of {{ill|Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001}} ({{ill|1691|Q7682|qid=Q7682}}), he inquired about the locations of the seven Tenjin shrines and inspected seven mounds then known collectively as “Seven-Generation Tenjin.” He advised that they be unified into a single shrine, and in the sixth year of Genroku ({{ill|1693|Q7689|qid=Q7689}}) the shrine buildings were constructed at the present location and the deities enshrined together {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. Mitsukuni also had a plaque reading “Seven-Generation Tenjingū” hung on the torii gate and dedicated sacred treasures {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}. During the Edo period, the shrine held 6 koku and 5 to of shrine land, and 9 koku, 9 to, and 3 shō as tax-exempt land {{Sfn|Inamura Shrine (Heibonsha)|1982}}.

In the {{ill|Meiji era|ar|فترة مييجي|ast|Dómina Meiji|az|Meydzi dövrü|azb|مئی‌جی دؤورو|be|Перыяд Мэйдзі|bn|মেইজি যুগ|bo|མེའི་ཇིའི་དུས་དུས་མཚམས།|ca|Era Meiji|cs|Období Meidži|da|Meiji-perioden|de|Meiji-Zeit|el|Μεϊτζί (περίοδος)|es|Era Meiji|et|Meiji periood|eu|Meiji Aroa|fa|دوره میجی|fi|Meiji-kausi|fr|Ère Meiji|gl|Período Meiji|he|תקופת מייג'י|hr|Meiji (razdoblje)|ht|Epòk Meiji|hu|Meidzsi-kor|id|Zaman Meiji|io|Ero Meiji|is|Meiji-tímabilið|it|Periodo Meiji|ja|明治|ka|მეიძის ეპოქა|kbp|Mejii wɛɛ yaa alɩwaatʊ|kk|Мэйдзи дәуірі|ko|메이지 시대|la|Aetas Meiji|lt|Meidži laikotarpis|lv|Meidzi periods|mk|Меиџи (период)|mn|Мэйжийн эрин|ms|Zaman Meiji|nl|Meijiperiode|nn|Meiji|no|Meiji-perioden|pl|Meiji (okres)|pt|Era Meiji|ro|Perioada Meiji|ru|Мэйдзи|simple|Meiji period|sk|Obdobie Meidži|sq|Periudha Meixhi|sr|Меиџи период|sv|Meijiperioden|ta|மெய்சி காலம்|th|ยุคเมจิ|tl|Panahong Meiji|tr|Meiji Dönemi|uk|Період Мейдзі|ur|میجی دور|vi|Thời kỳ Minh Trị|war|Panahon Meiji|wuu|明治|zh|明治|zh_classical|明治|zh_min_nan|Bêng-tī|zh_yue|明治|qid=Q3125096}}, the shrine was identified with the Shikinaisha Inamura Shrine and its name was changed from “Seven-Generation Tenjingū”<ref>[Archived link] Inamura Shrine (Research on Engishiki Shrines, personal website).</ref>. Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=modern shrine ranking system}}, it was ranked as a {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}.
